name: Christian asceticism and monastic promotion
plain_explanation: Both Jerome and Ambrose actively promoted celibacy, virginity, and withdrawal from worldly and sexual life as the highest form of Christian virtue, treating these as more urgent priorities than addressing the political collapse of Rome.
precise_definition: The promotion, especially by Jerome, of virginity and monastic/eremitic withdrawal as spiritually superior to ordinary life, expressed in treatises praising virginity and deprecating remarriage, and in Jerome's intense personal cultivation of aristocratic female converts (Paula, Eustochium) toward the ascetic life.
why_it_mattered: Russell finds it striking, and implicitly indicts it, that the most learned men of the age were more preoccupied with virginity and dietary/sexual purity than with the practical crisis of Rome's collapse.
historical_origin: Part of a broader fourth-century Christian ascetic movement (developed further in Chapter VI's account of monasticism).
examples: Jerome's letter to Eustochium using erotic mysticism to describe her spiritual marriage to Christ
Jerome's dream in which Christ condemns him as 'a follower of Cicero and not of Christ,' leading him to renounce classical literature for years
influence_on_later_thinkers: Anticipates the fuller treatment of monasticism as an institution in Chapter VI (Saint Benedict).
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Reflects the era's broader turn away from civic/political engagement toward otherworldly religious priorities, which Russell connects to Rome's decline.
